title: How medical neglect killed Alfredo Díaz in a Venezuelan cell
content:
The state deprived a former governor of medical care despite clear warning signs

Originally published on Global Voices

Illustration made with AI by Runrunes. Used with permission.

Read our special coverage on Venezuela’s fight for democracy and the political crisis that has unfolded since the 2024 presidential elections, after the documented allegations of electoral fraud.

This is the first installment of a series by Luis Carlos Díaz covering cases of torture, neglect, and cruel treatment against political prisoners, based on the latest report by the UN Fact-Finding Mission. Originally published in Runrunes and translated by Caracas Chronicles. 

To kick off this series, it is worth examining how the latest report by the UN Fact-Finding Mission (FFM) on Venezuela was constructed. Based on 213 confidential interviews with 121 victims, relatives, and witnesses, as well as forensic data and judicial documents, the report matches the rigorous evidentiary threshold of “reasonable grounds to believe.”

title: Trinbagonian Jason Jones wins landmark Privy Council judgement deeming ‘buggery laws’ unconstitutional
content:
‘The law finally caught up with basic human dignity’

Originally published on Global Voices

Trinbagonian LGBTQ+ activist Jason Jones at the Hall of Justice in Port of Spain, Trinidad, after the landmark 2018 judgement that deemed Trinidad and Tobago’s ‘buggery laws’ unconstitutional. Photo by Maria Nunes, used with permission.

Eight years and nearly seven months after Justice Devindra Rampersad ruled, in the case of LGBTQ+ activist Jason Jones vs. the Attorney General of Trinidad and Tobago, that Sections 13 and 16 of Trinidad and Tobago’s Sexual Offences Act Chapter 11:28 — which criminalise anal sex between consenting adults — were “unconstitutional,” the United Kingdom’s Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, still Trinidad and Tobago’s highest appellate court, overturned a 2025 Court of Appeal decision to keep the country’s “buggery law” on the books.
snippet:
‘The law finally caught up with basic human dignity’

title: Ecuadorian youth unite against neoliberal models and state violence
content:
Students are demanding a just future for all

Originally published on Global Voices

Screenshot of X video of the October 10, 2026 protest in Quito, Ecuador. Video by X user Elena Rodríguez. Fair Use.

This post is part of Global Voices’ November 2026 Spotlight series, “Justice as infrastructure.” In this Spotlight, Global Voices is partnering with The Hague Institute for Innovation of Law (HiiL) to highlight the ways justice functions as critical infrastructure for any society. You can support this coverage by donating here.

In Quito, in defiance of the Jóvenes en Acción (Youth in Action) strategy with which Daniel Noboa’s government has attempted to boost employment for young people, thousands of students have been staging marches and sit-ins in streets and squares, demanding medicines, security, and a budget for education.

title: Can regenerative school gardens strengthen food security in Cameroon?
content:
The school gardens are helping alleviate food insecurity while providing learning opportunities and empowering community members

Originally published on Global Voices

Students of Blessed Bilingual Education Centre preparing the farm. Photo by Support Humanity Cameroon. Used with permission.

Students of Blessed Bilingual Education Centre in Ebang, Cameroon’s Centre Region, have recorded their first harvest of the 2026–2027 school year. Through the Climate Change and Innovation Club, an initiative introduced in 2024 by Support Humanity Cameroon (SUHUCAM) to connect environmental education with practical action, students planted huckleberry in their school garden at the start of the academic year in September. Like them, pupils in Cameroon’s North West Region are managing school gardens and growing food using regenerative practices such as minimal tillage, composting, organic manure and fruit-tree grafting.
snippet:
The school gardens are helping alleviate food insecurity while providing learning opportunities and empowering community members

title: Justice is the infrastructure the world keeps forgetting
content:
The world cannot build prosperous economies, peaceful societies or resilient democracies while neglecting its people’s everyday justice needs.

Originally published on Global Voices

Image courtesy HiiL

This post by Jude Udo Ilo is part of Global Voices’ November 2026 Spotlight series, “Justice as infrastructure.” In this Spotlight, Global Voices is partnering with The Hague Institute for Innovation of Law (HiiL) to highlight the ways justice functions as critical infrastructure for any society. You can support this coverage by donating here.

Imagine visiting a hospital with a serious illness, only to discover that every patient receives the same medication, regardless of their symptoms. We would rightly call this a failure of healthcare. Yet this is remarkably close to how justice is delivered in much of the world.

We have built justice systems around institutions rather than people, procedures rather than problems, and legal traditions rather than lived realities. We measure progress by the number of courts constructed, judges appointed and laws enacted, while paying insufficient attention to whether ordinary people can actually resolve the disputes disrupting their lives.
snippet:
The world cannot build prosperous economies, peaceful societies or resilient democracies while neglecting its people’s everyday justice needs.

title: Restoring social media access comes at a cost in Gabon
content:
Citizens in Gabon went 248 days without access to Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, or YouTube

Originally published on Global Voices

Image of a smartphone showing the Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, YouTube, and Messenger apps. Screenshot from the DW Afrique YouTube channel.

After more than eight months of government blockage, Gabon has restored its social media access. But it has come at a cost. This reinstatement comes with a tighter regulatory framework and an unprecedented cooperation between the government and various tech giants, raising serious concerns about freedom of expression and privacy.

On February 17, 2026, Gabon’s media regulator, the High Communication Authority (HAC), suspended major social media networks, including Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, and YouTube, “until further notice.” According to the regulator, quoted in the daily newspaper L’Essentiel, this measure targeted not only content “undermining national security” but also content involving defamation, cyberbullying, hate speech, and threats to social cohesion.
snippet:
Citizens in Gabon went 248 days without access to Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, or YouTube

title: In Ukraine, youth are finding their voices in the digital democracy
content:
They are learning how to be drivers of change locally

Originally published on Global Voices

Participants of the Voices of Democracy project in Kyiv, Ukraine. Photo by beYOUnd. Used with permission.

This interview is part of a series of spotlights on the work of some of the grantees of the Digital Spark granting scheme, as part of the Regional Support Mechanism EECA project, implemented by the Metamorphosis Foundation and TechSoup, in partnership with CIVICUS and under the Digital Democracy Initiative (DDI) that covers the Global South. It is being published on Global Voices as part of a content-sharing agreement. 

The war in Ukraine has created a myriad of challenges for youth and their participation in public life and democratic processes, bringing displacement and misinformation as well as decreased opportunities for political engagement, economic activity, and access to information. At the same time, there are still avenues youth can pursue to contribute to political decisions and shape the fate of their communities.
snippet:
They are learning how to be drivers of change locally

title: Ex-lawmaker sentenced to 12.5 years in prison in closed-door trial in Macau
content:
Au Kam San's international legal representative called the trial a ‘sham’ with ‘manufactured allegations’

Originally published on Global Voices

Au Kam San. Photo from Au Kam San's Facebook page.

This post is part of Global Voices’ November 2026 Spotlight series, “Justice as infrastructure.” In this Spotlight, Global Voices is partnering with The Hague Institute for Innovation of Law (HiiL) to highlight the ways justice functions as critical infrastructure for any society. You can support this coverage by donating here.

The Chinese territory of Macau recorded its first conviction under the city’s national security law on November 6, 2026, sentencing 69-year-old former lawmaker Au Kam San to 12.5 years in prison. The Macau Court of First Instance tried the case behind closed doors, and international observers and rights groups have criticized the verdict, calling it a “bogus prosecution” that included “serious violations of his right to a fair trial.” The case raises broader questions about how justice is carried out in Macau, and whether its courts offer a fair, open way to challenge the state.
snippet:
Au Kam San's international legal representative called the trial a ‘sham’ with ‘manufactured allegations’

title: From a quiet life to the terror of armed gangs: The story of Haiti’s Kenscoff district
content:
On October 19, a unit of Salvadoran soldiers was also ambushed; the situation remains tense

Originally published on Global Voices

View of the hills from the road from Port-au-Prince to Kenscoff. Photo by Ketounette via Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 3.0).

In the heights of Pétion-Ville, more than 1,500 metres above sea level, sits the municipality of Kenscoff. A rural area just 20 kilometres (12.4 miles) southeast of downtown Port-au-Prince, Kenscoff is an idyllic contradiction of sorts. Its breathtaking landscape is dominated by pine trees and mountain ridges, dotted with terraced gardens and agricultural fields that supply fruit, vegetables and flowers to Port-au-Prince markets, grocery chains and restaurants. Yet, because of its high elevation, it can also get very cold and foggy, with the sun often setting by five in the afternoon.

The majority of Kenscoff’s residents are peasant farmers, though some wealthy Haitians, craving more peace, quiet, and fresh air, have chosen to leave the nearby urban areas of Port-au-Prince and Pétion-Ville for the area’s pastoral charm and community spirit.

On October 19, a unit of Salvadoran soldiers was also ambushed; the situation remains tense

title: Big Tech, AI, and the quiet expansion of digital surveillance in Nigeria
content:
How much control do people retain over their personal information in a world increasingly shaped by AI?

Originally published on Global Voices

Illustration by Nshua Cali-Dibang. Used with permission.

This post is part of Global Voices’ October 2026 Spotlight series, “Big Tech and Authoritarianism.” In this Spotlight, we explore how Big Tech facilitates and hinders authoritarian governments and practices, and how these choices influence the Global South. You can support this coverage by donating here.

Every search, social media interaction, and conversation with an artificial intelligence (AI) tool can leave behind information about its user. Individually, these digital traces may appear insignificant. Collectively, however, they can reveal interests, habits, preferences and patterns of behavior that have considerable commercial and political value.

How much control do people retain over their personal information in a world increasingly shaped by AI?

title: The dreamer who wants the world to read Nepali literature
content:
‘We no longer see Nepali literature as something confined by geographical boundaries.’

Originally published on Global Voices

Rishi Ram Adhikari delivering a speech at the Kitab Jatra Festival held in London in August 2026. Photo by Kushal Shrestha. Used with permission.

The Kitab Jatra Festival has quickly become one of the most vibrant platforms for celebrating Nepali literature, books and culture. The Festival is organised and hosted by the Kitab Yatra Foundation, a Nepal-based organisation promoting literature, reading, art and cultural exchange. Since its launch in 2018, the festival has grown from a local gathering into a dynamic international event, connecting readers and writers not only across Nepal but also in India, the UK, and the USA, with plans to expand to Dubai, Australia, Portugal, Belgium and Germany. Working in collaboration with various organisations and institutions, it has created a global stage where Nepali voices are shared, celebrated and amplified.
snippet:
‘We no longer see Nepali literature as something confined by geographical boundaries.’

title: Beyond the beaches: The Dominican Republic and the global debate over deep-sea mining
content:
The challenge is not solely to declare new protected areas, but ensure they have effective management

Originally published on Global Voices

The stunning beauty of the Dominican Republic’s north coast at Los Haitises National Park. Photo by Jason Boldero on Flickr (CC BY 2.0).

When you think of the Dominican Republic, the first thing that might come to mind is paradise where sun, sand, and sea combine to offer unforgettable experiences to Dominican families and global travellers alike — but the country’s deep sea is also of critical importance.

Jonathan Delance, director of conservation of the National 30×30 Program of the Ministry of Environment and Natural Resources, says that Dominican marine ecosystems are one of the country’s “greatest natural and strategic riches” — diverse, highly connected, and fundamental to national life.

From an ecological standpoint, coral reefs, mangroves, seagrass beds, dunes, beaches, pelagic zones, and deep-sea ecosystems sustain biodiversity. From an economic and social standpoint, they are the foundation of tourism, fishing, and coastal protection.
snippet:
The challenge is not solely to declare new protected areas, but ensure they have effective management

title: How people in Montenegro are making their country cleaner
content:
And helping to make the goals for EU accession plausible 

Originally published on Global Voices

Screenshot from the EkoMapa website of the EkoGard organization in Montenegro. Fair use.

This interview is part of a series of spotlights on the work of some of the grantees of the Digital Spark granting scheme, as part of the Regional Support Mechanism EECA project, implemented by the Metamorphosis Foundation and TechSoup, in partnership with CIVICUS and under the Digital Democracy Initiative (DDI) that covers the Global South. It is being published on Global Voices as part of a content-sharing agreement. 

Montenegro is on its way to joining the EU; at the moment, the goal is to do so by 2028. The United Nations Economic Commission for Europe (UNECE) review in 2025 states that the country has made significant progress in aligning its environmental legal and regulatory framework, as well as much of its national legislation, with European Union (EU) directives. 

However, some problems remain, including waste management and a very low recycling rate —  less than 2 percent, far below the EU’s 50 percent target.
snippet:
And helping to make the goals for EU accession plausible

title: Venezuela welcomes opposition leader María Corina Machado home
content:
Machado returns to a hopeful, cautious nation

Originally published on Global Voices

María Corina Machado arriving in Caracas after months of hiding and exile. Photo by Óscar Calles, 2026. Used with permission.

Thousands of people took to the Valle-Coche highway in Caracas to welcome the opposition leader and Nobel Peace Prize laureate María Corina Machado, who returned to Venezuela after 16 months in hiding and ten months in exile. The massive gathering was one of celebration, but her compatriots were also filled with doubts about what comes next.
snippet:
Machado returns to a hopeful, cautious nation

title: Global Voices condemns the attacks on Albanian fact-checking service Faktoje
content:
Faktoje is a respected member of the international fact-checking community

Originally published on Global Voices

Since October 27, at least 20 online media outlets and social media accounts in Albania have been waging a coordinated attack against the staff of fact-checking media service Faktoje Center, based in Tirana. A partner of Global Voices, Faktoje has been promoting accountability based on the right to information and transparency since 2018.

Faktoje and its team members, in particular its director, Klodiana Kapo, are facing a series of coordinated attacks from media outlets that have been circulating and reproducing articles that question Faktoje’s funding, financial management and independence, using its publicly available financial statements to cast doubt on the organisation’s credibility.
snippet:
Faktoje is a respected member of the international fact-checking community
